meta.desc.index: Gitflow lab for the mini-course: long-lived branches, release cycle, tags and changelog.
meta.desc.docs: Quick guide to the Gitflow workflow used in this mini-course: commands, PR targets and the release cycle.
hero.sub: The lab on the other side of the comparison. Here nothing goes straight to main: all work goes through develop, becomes a release/*, gets a tag and only then is published.
modelo.intro: Two branches live forever (main and develop). The others are born, fulfil a role and die. The path from an idea to production necessarily goes through all of them.
modelo.svg.titulo: Gitflow diagram: a feature branches off develop, returns to develop, enters a release branch and is published to main with a tag
branches.titulo: What branches from where, and what returns to where
branches.intro: This table is the rule of the game in this repository. Picking the wrong Pull Request target is the most common mistake for people starting with Gitflow.
branches.main: Always reflects what is published. Every commit here has a tag.
branches.develop: Where the team's work accumulates until it forms the next version.
branches.feature: One task. Never talks to main directly.
branches.release: Freeze scope, adjust version and changelog, fix the last details.
branches.hotfix: Production emergency, without waiting for the next release.
release.intro: Compare it mentally with the trunk-based repository: there, publishing is git push. Here there are six steps — and this is exactly the cost you need to feel in order to decide when it is worth it.
release.p1.texto: release/1.1.0 is created from develop. From here on, no new feature enters this version.
release.p2.texto: VERSION and CHANGELOG.md are updated on the release branch.
release.p3.texto: Only fixes go in. Each one is also taken back to develop.
release.p4.texto: Merge into main → the deploy Action puts the version online.
release.p5.texto: A v1.1.0 tag and a GitHub Release are created automatically from the CHANGELOG.
release.p6.texto: Back-merge from main to develop, so the fix is not lost in the next version.
participantes.intro: Same pattern as the trunk-based repository: one file per person in data/participantes/. What changes here is not the file — it is the path it takes to go live.
participantes.vazio: Nobody here yet — be the first person to add a file in data/participantes/.
participantes.erro: Could not load the list. Run "node scripts/gerar-manifesto.mjs" and serve the folder with a local HTTP server.
contribuir.nota: Your commit only shows up on the site when the next version is published — and that is a characteristic of the model, not a defect. Details in CONTRIBUTING.md.
docs.sub: Enough to work in this repository without picking the wrong Pull Request target.
docs.r1.texto: main is what is published; develop is what will be published. Everything else is temporary and must be deleted after the merge.
docs.r2.titulo: 2. You never commit directly to main or develop
docs.r2.texto: Always from a feature/*, with a Pull Request. Both permanent branches are protected — direct pushes are rejected by GitHub.
docs.r3.titulo: 3. The PR target depends on where the branch came from
docs.r3.texto: feature/* → develop. release/* and hotfix/* → main, and then back to develop. CI rejects the PR if the target is wrong.
docs.r4.titulo: 4. A version is a decision, not a consequence
docs.r4.texto: The number in VERSION only changes inside a release/* or hotfix/* branch. Your feature never touches it — it touches CHANGELOG.md, in the Unreleased section.
docs.r5.titulo: 5. What went into main must return to develop
docs.r5.texto: Fixes made in a release or hotfix need the back-merge, otherwise they reappear as a bug in the next version. Here that becomes an automatic PR.
docs.doeu.intro: Keep these observations for the final discussion of the mini-course — they are the material for the comparison with the trunk-based repository:
docs.q1: How much time passed between your commit and it showing up on the site?
docs.q2: How many steps did it take to publish a one-line change?
docs.q3: Did your branch conflict? How many days old was it?
docs.q4: On the upside: could you say exactly which version contains each change?
docs.q5: And could you roll the whole site back to a previous version with one command?
erro404.titulo: This page didn't make it into the release
erro404.sub: The address you looked for does not exist in this published version. Maybe it is still on develop, waiting for the next cycle.
desv.sub: Control and predictability come at a price. Understand why too many branches, release ceremonies and late integrations make Gitflow a bottleneck for teams that aim for continuous delivery.
desv.custos.intro: During the lab you felt first-hand the extra effort needed to put a simple change online. Below are the classic problems of this model.
desv.c1.p: A change that is ready on feature/* does not go live when it is done: it stays held on develop waiting for the next release/* to be opened and stabilized.
desv.c2.p: Branches that live for days or weeks diverge silently. When the whole team tries to integrate into develop or update CHANGELOG.md, conflicts are bigger and more complex.
desv.c3.p: Publishing requires freezing scope, creating a release/* branch, running version scripts, approving a PR to main, generating a tag and still doing the back-merge to develop.
desv.c4.p: Fixes made in release/* or hotfix/* must go back to develop. Without automation, it is common to forget this step and reintroduce the bug in the next version.
desv.c5.p: Beginners often open Pull Requests targeting the wrong branch (e.g. feature/* straight to main) or forget which base each type of branch must start from.
desv.c6.p: Continuous Integration assumes integrating code into the main trunk several times a day. With multiple layers of permanent branches, real production feedback is always postponed.
desv.anatomia.intro: See where the team's time and effort go between writing a line of code and publishing it to production:
desv.a1.p: While the branch lives apart, the rest of the team changes the base on develop without conflicts showing up immediately.
desv.a2.p: Even after the PR is reviewed and merged, the feature piles up in an intermediate environment, delivering no value to the end user.
desv.a3.p: The team has to coordinate a pause to prepare VERSION, close CHANGELOG.md and test a large batch of accumulated changes.
desv.a4.p: A production emergency requires creating hotfix/* from main, bumping the patch version and handling two separate merges (main and develop).
desv.comp.intro: A direct comparison of the operational cost you experienced in the two repositories of the mini-course:
desv.comp.r2.t: Direct commit or short PR to main
desv.comp.r3.t: git revert or a quick fix straight on main
desv.evitar.titulo: When to avoid (and when to still use it)
desv.evitar.intro: Gitflow's own creator, Vincent Driessen, added a note years later recommending trunk-based flows for modern web applications with continuous delivery.
desv.evitar.nao1: Your product is a web application or SaaS with only one active version in production.
desv.evitar.nao2: Your team practices Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Delivery (CD) daily.
desv.evitar.nao3: The team is small and the release ceremony takes more time than development.
desv.evitar.nao4: You need to validate hypotheses and fix production problems within minutes.
desv.evitar.ok1: You ship packaged software (mobile apps with store review, desktop, firmware).
desv.evitar.ok2: You must maintain and support multiple older versions at the same time (v1.x, v2.x).
desv.evitar.ok3: The project requires formal auditing, strict acceptance windows and manual release approval.
desv.evitar.ok4: The repository is open, with dozens of contributors who have no prior context on the project.
meta.desc.desv: Analysis of the drawbacks, operational costs and pitfalls of the Gitflow model compared to Trunk-Based Development.
conclusao.intro: GitFlow is not obsolete, but it has become a niche model. It is no longer the default choice for most modern technology companies (SaaS and Web), but it remains irreplaceable in scenarios that demand strict version control.
conclusao.citacao:
"If your software requires supporting multiple versions in production at the same time, or if you have a traditional release cycle, GitFlow may still be the right choice. But for web applications that are updated continuously, simpler flows such as GitHub Flow are more suitable."
— Vincent Driessen, creator of GitFlow (reflection added in 2020)
conclusao.pros1: Impeccable organization: Excellent for managing releases of specific, well-defined versions (e.g. Version 1.0, 2.0).
conclusao.pros2: Security and auditing: Ideal for highly regulated environments (banking, healthcare) that require multiple tests and human approvals.
conclusao.pros3: Protected production: The main branch stays fully isolated from the chaos of day-to-day development.
conclusao.contras.t: When Does It Become a Problem?
conclusao.contras1: Merge hell: Keeping branches apart for too long creates massive, complex conflicts when merging the code.
conclusao.contras2: Incompatible with CI/CD: It slows down the deploy process, going against the modern culture of shipping updates several times a day.
conclusao.contras3: Unnecessary bureaucracy: For small teams or simple projects, opening and closing 5 types of branches creates useless complexity.
meta.desc.conclusao: Concluding analysis of GitFlow: pros, cons, ideal usage scenarios and reflections on its viability in modern development.
